Use systems to manage the work. Use humanity to lead the people. That is the balance. You do not manage people as if they are spreadsheets, and you do not lead operations with vague inspiration alone. Effective leaders know when to be analytical and when to be relational.  Patient experience lives at the intersection of systems and emotions.   A patient's experience is shaped by operational realities: how easy it is to schedule, how long they wait, how clearly billing is explained, how smoothly referrals happen, and how efficiently the visit flows. But the patient's experience is also shaped by human realities: whether they feel heard, respected, informed, valued, safe, and cared for.   Effective healthcare leadership requires both discipline and humanity. We manage from the left brain through systems, structure, data, and accountability. We lead from the right brain through empathy, vision, communication, and trust. (Melissa)","channel":"LinkedIn — Personal","theme":"Personal — Healthcare Leadership","ctype":"Single Post","funnel":"Nurture (Existing audience)","title":"The Miracle Morning","message":"I needed to fix my morning routine.  Not tweak it.  Fix it.  Somewhere in the chaos of growing a business, managing responsibilities, and trying to keep all the moving pieces moving, my mornings had become unfocused.  I would get up, pour my coffee, open my computer, and immediately get pulled into whatever project was already on my mind.  One email turned into one task.  One task turned into one rabbit hole.  Before I knew it, I was rushing through my workout or cutting pieces of it short.  That is not me.  I am regimented. I love structure. I function best with a routine.  But even disciplined people can drift when life gets cluttered.  So I thought back to a time when my mornings felt focused, unrushed, and purposeful. It was right after I read *The Miracle Morning* by Hal Elrod.  The framework is S.A.V.E.R.S.:  **Silence** **Affirmation** **Visualization** **Exercise** **Reading** **Scribing**  Sixty minutes a day.  It does not have to happen in that exact order. For me, exercise comes at the end because I want space for a full workout, not a rushed version of one.  The point is not perfection.  The point is intention.  Because how I start my morning affects how I lead, how I think, how I respond, and how I move through the rest of the day.  I do not want to start my day reacting.  I want to start my day grounded.  So I am getting back to the routine that works.  If your mornings feel frantic, rushed, or chaotic, I would encourage you to read the book and try the S.A.V.E.R.S. routine for 30 days. often assume that because of this collection of medals, I love to push my limits. They're right.  I've completed races ranging from 5Ks to marathons, triathlons, 24-hour relays, and an Ironman. I know how to train. I know how to push through discomfort. I know how to keep going when my body wants to quit.  I know how to grind.  But lately, I've been reminded that growth isn't always about pushing harder. Sometimes it's about stepping back.  I'm an avid Peloton user, and I love their training programs. Recently, I started the Progression Run program. Ironically, it's designed for beginner runners.  I'm not a beginner.  So why would I choose it?  Because I needed a reset. I wanted to return to the foundation. To slow down. To pay attention to form. To focus on breathing, cadence, pacing, and consistency instead of speed.  There were moments when the coach said, \"Recovery pace.\"  Every instinct told me I could go faster. But I didn't.  I trusted the process. I followed the coaching.  Because sometimes discipline isn't pushing harder. Sometimes discipline is resisting the urge to.  Leadership is no different.  As we gain experience, it's easy to believe we've outgrown the fundamentals. We stop listening as closely. We skip steps. We rely on what we've always done. But the best leaders I know never stop returning to the basics.  They sharpen their communication. They strengthen relationships. They revisit accountability. They seek feedback. They stay coachable.  You don't build excellence by constantly chasing the next advanced technique. You build it by mastering the fundamentals over and over again. Workarounds can look like commitment. They can also hide risk. This is not only a communication issue. It is a workflow issue. Healthcare teams are under pressure to move quickly. The goal is not to slow the system down. The goal is to design a system where efficiency and care can coexist. Leaders shape culture by what they measure, coach, praise, and tolerate. Workflow improvement is not only about efficiency. It is about reducing unnecessary friction so teams can bring more presence, patience, and compassion to the moments that matter. A compassionate workflow makes the right thing easier to do. It helps staff anticipate needs, communicate clearly, reduce patient effort, and recover quickly when something goes wrong. It does not rely on memory, personality, or heroic effort. It creates reliable conditions for care. In healthcare, compassion is often described as a behavior. It is also an operating principle. When the workflow supports the behavior, the culture becomes more consistent. That is why patient experience improvement cannot be separated from operational improvement. A metric can focus attention. It can also narrow attention. If teams are measured only on speed, they may rush. If they are measured only on satisfaction, they may avoid hard conversations. month.","message":"","ctaType":"","ctaLink":"","status":"published","priority":"","repFrom":"","postUrl":"","owner":"Melissa","connected":"","handoff":"","caption":"As I reflect on that milestone, I’m thinking about more than the business I’ve built. I’m thinking about how the work has changed, and how it has changed me.\nI started HMCG because I wanted to help close the gap between how healthcare practices intend to deliver care and how patients actually experience it.\nAfter years in healthcare operations, I understood that good intentions were not enough. Practices needed processes that worked, leaders who were supported, and a clear connection between the decisions made behind the scenes and the experience of the person receiving care. I wanted to help make that connection.\nOver these three years, the focus has become sharper. Operations, leadership, and patient experience cannot be treated as separate priorities. A scheduling process is a patient experience. A leadership decision shapes the staff experience. Both influence the relationship a patient develops with a practice.\nThat perspective has taken shape through the Nine Pillars of Patient Experience Framework, the PX360 Assessment, and the conversations we’re having on TouchPoints. Alongside HMCG, my work through The Focused Leader has extended that focus to supporting the people responsible for leading change.\nI’ve grown alongside the business, too.\nDeveloping a framework, writing, hosting a podcast, and coaching leaders have challenged me to clarify my thinking, question my assumptions, and learn from people whose experiences differ from mine. They have also given me new ways to contribute beyond the work I do directly with a practice.\nOne commitment I’m carrying forward is that the value of this work should last beyond an engagement. I want to help leaders and teams build the clarity, confidence, and capability to keep improving, rather than becoming dependent on someone else to supply every answer.\nThe next chapter of HMCG builds on that foundation: deeper patient experience work, practical tools that help practices act on what they learn, and stronger support for the leaders turning strategy into daily decisions.\nThe goal is to help practices become places where accountability and compassion work together for patients, staff, and the people leading them.\nTo the clients who have trusted me, the colleagues who have challenged and encouraged me, and everyone who has read, listened, shared, or joined a conversation: thank you. Your motivation isn’t unlimited. Protect both.\n\nHave you ever left a role that looked great on paper? Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Highlights cross-functional breakdowns","caption":"Friday Field Note: Patients often judge the experience at the transition points. The handoff from call center to clinic. The move from waiting room to exam room. The shift from visit to follow-up. The moment after a test result. The discharge instruction that determines confidence at home. Transitions reveal whether the organization is coordinated. When transitions are unclear, patients feel the burden of the system. When transitions are designed well, patients feel guided. A culture of care pays attention to these moments because they are where trust can either strengthen or weaken quickly. The experience is rarely one moment. It is the connection between moments.","cta":"Choose one transition point and ask patients and staff what feels unclear.","visual":"Patient journey line with transition moments highlighted","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #CareCoordination"},{"n":15,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Practical fix for uncertainty and perceived wait","caption":"The Friday Fix: Create a start-of-visit expectation standard. At the beginning of the encounter, patients should know three things: What will happen today. Who they will interact with. What should happen after the visit. This does not require a long script. It requires consistency. When expectations are clear, patients feel more oriented and staff spend less time answering preventable questions later. A culture of care is built through small moments of clarity repeated reliably. This week, ask: Do patients know what to expect before they have to ask?","cta":"Test this standard with one department or clinic team next week.","visual":"Three-part expectation card: Today, Team, Next Step","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientEngagement"},{"n":16,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Connects patient confidence to workflow reliability","caption":"What good looks like: discharge with confidence. A patient should not leave wondering what to do next, who to call, or what warning signs matter. A strong discharge experience is clear, teachable, and supported by follow-up. The team confirms understanding, avoids unnecessary jargon, and makes the next step visible. The patient leaves with confidence. The staff leave knowing the message was understood. This is not only a communication issue. It is a workflow issue. A culture of care ensures the final moments of an encounter are not rushed, confusing, or dependent on memory alone.","cta":"Review one discharge or after-visit process through the patient’s eyes.","visual":"Discharge checklist with confidence cues","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #DischargePlanning"},{"n":17,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Questions incentive and performance alignment","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Is your culture rewarding speed over care? Healthcare teams are under pressure to move quickly. But when speed becomes the only visible priority, patients may experience rushed communication and staff may feel forced to choose between compassion and throughput. The goal is not to slow the system down. The goal is to design a system where efficiency and care can coexist. Leaders shape culture by what they measure, coach, praise, and tolerate. Ask this week: Are our operational expectations helping staff deliver care well, or forcing them to recover after the process fails?","cta":"Use this question in your next manager meeting.","visual":"Balance scale: Efficiency and Care","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareLeadership"},{"n":18,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Links culture, burnout, and workflow design","caption":"Friday Field Note: Rework has a culture cost. When staff spend the day correcting missing information, chasing answers, repeating instructions, or explaining process breakdowns, empathy becomes harder to sustain. This does not mean staff do not care. It means the system is draining capacity that should be available for care. A culture of care must protect both patients and the people serving them. Workflow improvement is not only about efficiency. It is about reducing unnecessary friction so teams can bring more presence, patience, and compassion to the moments that matter. Operational design is emotional design.","cta":"Identify one source of avoidable rework that affects both patients and staff.","visual":"Rework loop showing staff capacity drain","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #EmployeeExperience"},{"n":19,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Offers a simple way to find communication gaps","caption":"The Friday Fix: Track the questions patients ask repeatedly. For one week, ask front-line teams to capture the top five questions they answer over and over. Then ask: Where should this information have been clearer? Which questions point to unclear instructions? Which questions point to process uncertainty? Which questions create avoidable call volume or front-desk pressure? Repeated questions are not interruptions. They are signals. They show where the patient journey needs better communication, better timing, or better design. When the process answers predictable questions early, everyone benefits.","cta":"Start with one team and collect repeated questions for five business days.","visual":"Top 5 patient questions tracker","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientCommunication"},{"n":20,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Frames operations as the infrastructure of care","caption":"What good looks like: compassionate workflows. A compassionate workflow makes the right thing easier to do. It helps staff anticipate needs, communicate clearly, reduce patient effort, and recover quickly when something goes wrong. It does not rely on memory, personality, or heroic effort. It creates reliable conditions for care. In healthcare, compassion is often described as a behavior. It is also an operating principle. When the workflow supports the behavior, the culture becomes more consistent. That is why patient experience improvement cannot be separated from operational improvement. The experience lives inside the workflow.","cta":"Use this language when connecting culture work to process improvement.","visual":"Workflow as the foundation under compassionate behaviors","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #CultureTransformation"},{"n":21,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Encourages metric and accountability review","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Are your metrics driving the behavior you actually want? A metric can focus attention. It can also narrow attention. If teams are measured only on speed, they may rush. If they are measured only on satisfaction, they may avoid hard conversations. If they are measured without context, they may disengage. Patient experience measurement should lead to learning, not blame. The leadership opportunity is to connect metrics to behaviors, workflows, and coaching. Ask: What do our measures encourage our teams to do every day? That answer matters to culture.","cta":"Review one patient experience metric and identify the behavior it is currently shaping.","visual":"Metric → Behavior → Experience chain","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareMetrics"},{"n":22,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Connects communication to trust and emotional experience","caption":"Friday Field Note: Silence creates anxiety. When patients do not know what is happening, when they will be seen, who is responsible, or what comes next, they begin filling in the gaps themselves. That uncertainty can make even a reasonable delay feel careless. A culture of care does not wait for patients to become frustrated before communicating. It builds proactive communication into the workflow. The message does not need to be complex. It needs to be timely, honest, and respectful. In many cases, the experience improves not because the wait disappeared, but because uncertainty did.","cta":"Identify one point where proactive communication could reduce patient anxiety.","visual":"Silence vs. clarity comparison card","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientTrust"},{"n":23,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Concrete process standard for a common pain point","caption":"The Friday Fix: Create a delay communication standard. Choose one setting where delays happen often. Define: When patients should be updated. Who is responsible for the update. What information should be shared. What options, if any, should be offered. How staff should escalate when the delay worsens. This is not scripting for the sake of scripting. It is consistency for the sake of trust. Patients should not have to ask to be informed. A culture of care anticipates predictable frustration and responds before it becomes a complaint.","cta":"Pilot this standard in one high-delay area for two weeks.","visual":"Delay communication standard template","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #ClinicFlow"},{"n":24,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Distinguishes rounding from visibility theater","caption":"What good looks like: leadership rounding that leads to improvement. Effective rounding is not only asking, “How is everything going?” It is listening for barriers, validating what teams experience, and closing the loop on what will change. Staff need to see that speaking up leads to action. Patients need to feel that leaders understand the real experience of care. A strong rounding process captures themes, assigns follow-up, and reports back. That is how rounding becomes more than visibility. It becomes a tool for culture, accountability, and operational learning. Care improves when leaders stay close to the work.","cta":"Add a close-the-loop step to your next rounding process.","visual":"Rounding loop: Listen → Capture → Act → Report back","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #LeadershipRounding"},{"n":25,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Invites leaders to examine psychological safety and process reliability","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Do frontline teams trust the escalation process? When staff know how to escalate and believe leadership will respond, small issues are less likely to become patient experience failures. When escalation feels unclear, slow, or punitive, staff often create workarounds or absorb the problem themselves. A culture of care depends on psychological safety and operational clarity. Ask your teams: When something is getting in the way of patient care, do you know exactly what to do next? Then ask the harder question: Do you believe the response will help?","cta":"Use these two questions in your next frontline listening session.","visual":"Escalation confidence scale","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PsychologicalSafety"},{"n":26,"type":"Score Behind the Score","theme":"HMCG - Client Lesson / Trend / Myth vs. Reality","note":"Moves prospects from measurement to consulting diagnosis","caption":"Score Behind the Score: The number is not the whole story. Patient experience scores can point leaders in the right direction, but they rarely explain the full cause. A low score may reflect communication, access, handoffs, expectations, staffing pressure, unclear accountability, or workflow friction. The score is the signal. The real work is diagnosis. Before moving directly to training, scripting, or reminders, ask: What is the experience behind the score? What workflow produced it? What support do staff need to change it reliably? Improvement starts when measurement becomes learning.","cta":"Use this lens before designing your next patient experience action plan.","visual":"Score → Signal → Diagnosis → Improvement pathway","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientExperienceStrategy"},{"n":27,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Expands patient experience beyond the visit","caption":"Friday Field Note: The patient experience starts before the patient arrives. It starts with the phone call, the portal message, the referral process, the instructions, the reminder, and the question of whether the patient knows what to do next. By the time someone reaches the front desk, they may already feel confident or frustrated. Access is not only an appointment slot. It is the ease, clarity, and reliability of getting to care. A culture of care pays attention to the pre-visit experience because it sets expectations before the clinical encounter begins. The visit does not start at check-in. It starts at first contact.","cta":"Review your pre-visit experience as part of your patient journey work.","visual":"Pre-visit journey timeline","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #AccessExperience"},{"n":28,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Tactical action for leadership visibility","caption":"The Friday Fix: Call your own phone line. Use a common patient scenario and test the experience. How long does it take to reach the right person? Are the options clear? What happens after hours? Can the patient resolve their need without being transferred repeatedly? Does the portal message create clarity or more work? Digital and phone access are often treated as separate from patient experience, but patients do not separate them. They experience one organization. This week, test one access path and document what the patient must figure out alone.","cta":"Ask one leader to complete this test and share the findings with the team.","visual":"Access test scorecard","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #DigitalHealth"},{"n":29,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Defines a clear operational win","caption":"What good looks like: first-contact resolution. When patients reach out, the best experience is not being politely transferred five times. It is being guided clearly, resolved efficiently, or connected to the right next step with context intact. First-contact resolution requires more than friendly service. It requires information access, clear decision rights, training, workflow design, and escalation pathways. The patient experiences competence. The staff experience clarity. A culture of care removes unnecessary loops. When the first contact is reliable, trust begins earlier and frustration is reduced before the patient ever walks through the door.","cta":"Assess whether your teams have the information and authority to resolve common requests.","visual":"First-contact resolution flow","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #OperationalEfficiency"},{"n":30,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Creates empathy and process awareness","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: What are patients expected to figure out alone? How to schedule. Where to park. What to bring. Which portal message matters. What the next step is. Who to call after the visit. Whether a delay is normal. What a bill means. Every unanswered question adds effort. A culture of care reduces avoidable effort by making the next step clear. Leaders can start by identifying where the organization assumes knowledge patients may not have. The experience improves when the system stops making patients translate the process for themselves.","cta":"Ask a patient advisory group or frontline team to identify the top unclear moments.","visual":"List graphic: Things patients should not have to figure out alone","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientCenteredCare"},{"n":31,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Moves culture from slogan to observable behavior","caption":"Friday Field Note: Culture is revealed under pressure. It is easy to describe care values when the schedule is on time, staffing is stable, and patients are calm. The real test is what happens when the day is behind, the waiting room is full, the phones are heavy, and the team is stretched. Do expectations stay clear? Do leaders support the team? Do patients still receive respectful communication? Do staff feel safe raising concerns? A culture of care is not proven by the words on the wall. It is proven by the behaviors the organization protects when pressure rises.","cta":"Observe one high-pressure period and note what the culture rewards.","visual":"Culture under pressure thermometer","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #WorkplaceCulture"},{"n":32,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Turns values into measurable behaviors","caption":"The Friday Fix: Define one care value in operational terms. Choose a value your organization uses often, such as respect, compassion, teamwork, or accountability. Then answer: What does this look like in patient communication? What does it look like during a delay? What does it look like in a handoff? What does it look like when a staff member needs help? What does it look like when expectations are missed? Values become culture when people know what they mean in daily work. This week, translate one value into observable behaviors.","cta":"Use this exercise with managers during your next culture discussion.","visual":"Value-to-behavior translation worksheet","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #CultureOfCare"},{"n":33,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Supports culture-building and leadership trust","caption":"What good looks like: accountability without blame. A strong culture of care does not avoid accountability. It makes accountability constructive. The question is not, “Who failed?” The better questions are: Was the expectation clear? Was the workflow realistic? Was the team trained and supported? Did leadership follow through? What needs to change so the right action becomes easier next time? Blame shuts down learning. Accountability strengthens learning. Healthcare teams need standards, coaching, and systems that make consistent care possible. That is how accountability becomes a culture builder instead of a fear trigger.","cta":"Use these questions when reviewing a patient experience miss.","visual":"Accountability questions framework","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #JustCulture"},{"n":34,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Targets operational constraint behind culture inconsistency","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Do your managers have time to coach the culture you want? Many organizations ask managers to improve patient experience, support staff, monitor metrics, resolve issues, and keep operations moving. Then they leave little time for observation, feedback, and development. Culture is reinforced through daily coaching. If managers are always reacting, the culture becomes reactive too. The leadership question is not only whether managers know what to coach. It is whether the operating model gives them space to coach consistently. A culture of care needs leadership capacity, not just leadership intention.","cta":"Review one manager role and identify what is crowding out coaching time.","visual":"Manager capacity pie chart concept","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareManagers"},{"n":35,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Shows that implementation happens in operations","caption":"Friday Field Note: Strategy succeeds or fails in the daily schedule. A patient experience strategy may be clear at the executive level, but the daily schedule determines whether teams can live it. Are there moments for communication? Is there time to recover after a service issue? Can staff complete follow-up reliably? Do managers have room to coach? Are expectations realistic during peak flow? Culture does not live in the strategy document. It lives in the workday. When the schedule leaves no room for care behaviors, the organization should not be surprised when those behaviors become inconsistent. Design the day to support the experience.","cta":"Look at one daily schedule and ask what care behaviors it enables or prevents.","visual":"Daily schedule with care moments highlighted","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #StrategyExecution"},{"n":36,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Practical low-lift observation tool","caption":"The Friday Fix: Take a 15-minute workflow walk. Choose one process and follow it in real time. Do not start with a meeting. Start with observation. Watch where staff pause, search, clarify, repeat, wait, or create a workaround. Then ask: What is making this harder than it needs to be? What does the patient experience because of it? What would make the right action easier? A short workflow walk can reveal more than a long report. Patient experience improvement often begins by seeing the work clearly.","cta":"Schedule one 15-minute workflow walk before next Friday.","visual":"Workflow walk checklist","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #ProcessImprovement"},{"n":37,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Connects patient flow and employee experience","caption":"What good looks like: patient flow that protects staff capacity. A well-designed flow does more than move patients faster. It reduces unnecessary confusion, rework, interruptions, and preventable escalation. Staff can focus. Patients receive clearer communication. Leaders see problems earlier. Teams have a shared understanding of what should happen next. Flow is not only a throughput issue. It is a care issue. When flow breaks down, staff absorb the friction and patients feel the impact. A culture of care designs operations so teams are not constantly recovering from avoidable breakdowns.","cta":"Evaluate one workflow for both patient impact and staff capacity impact.","visual":"Flow impact model: Patient clarity + Staff capacity","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientFlow"},{"n":38,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Reframes burnout from individual resilience to system design","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Is burnout being treated as an individual issue or a design signal? Resilience matters. Support matters. But if the same frustrations show up across teams, the organization should examine the work itself. What rework is constant? What processes create unnecessary emotional labor? Where do staff feel unsupported? Where does the patient experience depend on staff absorbing system friction? A culture of care must care for the caregivers by improving the conditions in which care is delivered. Burnout conversations should lead to operational questions, not only wellness reminders.","cta":"Ask teams what process drains the most energy and why.","visual":"Burnout signal map: Rework, ambiguity, interruptions, escalation","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareWorkforce"},{"n":39,"type":"Client Lesson / Field Lesson","theme":"HMCG - Client Lesson / Trend / Myth vs. Reality","note":"Demonstrates consulting insight from implementation","caption":"Field Lesson: Staff adoption improves when the workflow helps them too. Patient experience initiatives often struggle when they feel like one more thing added to an already full day. Adoption improves when teams can see how the change reduces confusion, prevents rework, clarifies expectations, or makes difficult conversations easier. The best improvements serve both patients and staff. That is why implementation should ask: What will this feel like for the patient? What will this feel like for the team? What support will make the new behavior sustainable? A culture of care cannot be bolted onto the work. It has to be built into the work.","cta":"Use this three-question test before rolling out your next experience initiative.","visual":"Patient benefit + Staff benefit = Sustainable adoption","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #ChangeManagement"},{"n":40,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Broadens experience work to clarity and inclusion","caption":"Friday Field Note: Equity and patient experience meet in the details. Instructions that are hard to understand. Processes that assume digital access. Phone systems that are difficult to navigate. Follow-up steps that require patients to know how healthcare works. These are experience issues. They can also become access issues. A culture of care asks whether the process is clear, usable, and respectful for the people it is intended to serve. Patient experience work should not only ask, “Was the patient satisfied?” It should also ask, “Was the experience understandable, navigable, and inclusive?”","cta":"Review one patient-facing process for clarity and usability.","visual":"Inclusive experience checklist","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthEquity"},{"n":41,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Simple action that improves communication and reduces calls","caption":"The Friday Fix: Review one patient instruction for clarity. The next step is diagnosis, prioritization, and action.","cta":"If these themes sound familiar, it may be time to assess the experience behind the scores.","visual":"Year-end insight to action roadmap","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareConsulting"}],"id":"hmcgfriday","questions":["Friday Field Note: Patients often judge the experience at the transition points. The handoff from call center to clinic. The move from waiting room to exam room. The shift from visit to follow-up. The moment after a test result. The discharge instruction that determines confidence at home. Transitions reveal whether the organization is coordinated. When transitions are unclear, patients feel the burden of the system. When transitions are designed well, patients feel guided. A culture of care pays attention to these moments because they are where trust can either strengthen or weaken quickly. The experience is rarely one moment. It is the connection between moments.","The Friday Fix: Create a start-of-visit expectation standard. At the beginning of the encounter, patients should know three things: What will happen today. Who they will interact with. What should happen after the visit. This does not require a long script. It requires consistency. When expectations are clear, patients feel more oriented and staff spend less time answering preventable questions later. A culture of care is built through small moments of clarity repeated reliably. This week, ask: Do patients know what to expect before they have to ask?","What good looks like: discharge with confidence. A patient should not leave wondering what to do next, who to call, or what warning signs matter. A strong discharge experience is clear, teachable, and supported by follow-up. The team confirms understanding, avoids unnecessary jargon, and makes the next step visible. The patient leaves with confidence. The staff leave knowing the message was understood. This is not only a communication issue. It is a workflow issue. A culture of care ensures the final moments of an encounter are not rushed, confusing, or dependent on memory alone.","Friday Leadership Reflection: Is your culture rewarding speed over care? Healthcare teams are under pressure to move quickly. But when speed becomes the only visible priority, patients may experience rushed communication and staff may feel forced to choose between compassion and throughput. The goal is not to slow the system down. The goal is to design a system where efficiency and care can coexist. Leaders shape culture by what they measure, coach, praise, and tolerate. Ask this week: Are our operational expectations helping staff deliver care well, or forcing them to recover after the process fails?","Friday Field Note: Rework has a culture cost. When staff spend the day correcting missing information, chasing answers, repeating instructions, or explaining process breakdowns, empathy becomes harder to sustain. This does not mean staff do not care. It means the system is draining capacity that should be available for care. A culture of care must protect both patients and the people serving them. Workflow improvement is not only about efficiency. It is about reducing unnecessary friction so teams can bring more presence, patience, and compassion to the moments that matter. Operational design is emotional design.","The Friday Fix: Track the questions patients ask repeatedly. For one week, ask front-line teams to capture the top five questions they answer over and over. Then ask: Where should this information have been clearer? Which questions point to unclear instructions? Which questions point to process uncertainty? Which questions create avoidable call volume or front-desk pressure? Repeated questions are not interruptions. They are signals. They show where the patient journey needs better communication, better timing, or better design. When the process answers predictable questions early, everyone benefits.","What good looks like: compassionate workflows. A compassionate workflow makes the right thing easier to do. It helps staff anticipate needs, communicate clearly, reduce patient effort, and recover quickly when something goes wrong. It does not rely on memory, personality, or heroic effort. It creates reliable conditions for care. In healthcare, compassion is often described as a behavior. It is also an operating principle. When the workflow supports the behavior, the culture becomes more consistent. That is why patient experience improvement cannot be separated from operational improvement. The experience lives inside the workflow.","Friday Leadership Reflection: Are your metrics driving the behavior you actually want? A metric can focus attention. It can also narrow attention. If teams are measured only on speed, they may rush. If they are measured only on satisfaction, they may avoid hard conversations. If they are measured without context, they may disengage. Patient experience measurement should lead to learning, not blame. The leadership opportunity is to connect metrics to behaviors, workflows, and coaching. Ask: What do our measures encourage our teams to do every day? That answer matters to culture.","Friday Field Note: Silence creates anxiety. When patients do not know what is happening, when they will be seen, who is responsible, or what comes next, they begin filling in the gaps themselves. That uncertainty can make even a reasonable delay feel careless. A culture of care does not wait for patients to become frustrated before communicating. It builds proactive communication into the workflow. The message does not need to be complex. It needs to be timely, honest, and respectful. In many cases, the experience improves not because the wait disappeared, but because uncertainty did.","The Friday Fix: Create a delay communication standard. Choose one setting where delays happen often. Define: When patients should be updated. Who is responsible for the update. What information should be shared. What options, if any, should be offered. How staff should escalate when the delay worsens. This is not scripting for the sake of scripting. It is consistency for the sake of trust. Patients should not have to ask to be informed. A culture of care anticipates predictable frustration and responds before it becomes a complaint.","What good looks like: leadership rounding that leads to improvement. Effective rounding is not only asking, “How is everything going?” It is listening for barriers, validating what teams experience, and closing the loop on what will change. Staff need to see that speaking up leads to action. Patients need to feel that leaders understand the real experience of care. A strong rounding process captures themes, assigns follow-up, and reports back. That is how rounding becomes more than visibility. It becomes a tool for culture, accountability, and operational learning. Care improves when leaders stay close to the work.","Friday Leadership Reflection: Do frontline teams trust the escalation process? When staff know how to escalate and believe leadership will respond, small issues are less likely to become patient experience failures. When escalation feels unclear, slow, or punitive, staff often create workarounds or absorb the problem themselves. A culture of care depends on psychological safety and operational clarity. Ask your teams: When something is getting in the way of patient care, do you know exactly what to do next? Then ask the harder question: Do you believe the response will help?","Score Behind the Score: The number is not the whole story. Patient experience scores can point leaders in the right direction, but they rarely explain the full cause. A low score may reflect communication, access, handoffs, expectations, staffing pressure, unclear accountability, or workflow friction. The score is the signal. The real work is diagnosis. Before moving directly to training, scripting, or reminders, ask: What is the experience behind the score? What workflow produced it? What support do staff need to change it reliably? Improvement starts when measurement becomes learning.","Friday Field Note: The patient experience starts before the patient arrives. It starts with the phone call, the portal message, the referral process, the instructions, the reminder, and the question of whether the patient knows what to do next. By the time someone reaches the front desk, they may already feel confident or frustrated. Access is not only an appointment slot. It is the ease, clarity, and reliability of getting to care. A culture of care pays attention to the pre-visit experience because it sets expectations before the clinical encounter begins. The visit does not start at check-in. It starts at first contact.","The Friday Fix: Call your own phone line. Use a common patient scenario and test the experience. How long does it take to reach the right person? Are the options clear? What happens after hours? Can the patient resolve their need without being transferred repeatedly? Does the portal message create clarity or more work? Digital and phone access are often treated as separate from patient experience, but patients do not separate them. They experience one organization. This week, test one access path and document what the patient must figure out alone.","What good looks like: first-contact resolution. When patients reach out, the best experience is not being politely transferred five times. It is being guided clearly, resolved efficiently, or connected to the right next step with context intact. First-contact resolution requires more than friendly service. It requires information access, clear decision rights, training, workflow design, and escalation pathways. The patient experiences competence. The staff experience clarity. A culture of care removes unnecessary loops. When the first contact is reliable, trust begins earlier and frustration is reduced before the patient ever walks through the door.","Friday Leadership Reflection: What are patients expected to figure out alone? How to schedule. Where to park. What to bring. Which portal message matters. What the next step is. Who to call after the visit. Whether a delay is normal. What a bill means. Every unanswered question adds effort. A culture of care reduces avoidable effort by making the next step clear. Leaders can start by identifying where the organization assumes knowledge patients may not have. The experience improves when the system stops making patients translate the process for themselves.","Friday Field Note: Culture is revealed under pressure. It is easy to describe care values when the schedule is on time, staffing is stable, and patients are calm. Do patients still receive respectful communication? Do staff feel safe raising concerns? A culture of care is not proven by the words on the wall. It is proven by the behaviors the organization protects when pressure rises.","The Friday Fix: Define one care value in operational terms. Choose a value your organization uses often, such as respect, compassion, teamwork, or accountability. Then answer: What does this look like in patient communication? Values become culture when people know what they mean in daily work. This week, translate one value into observable behaviors.","What good looks like: accountability without blame. A strong culture of care does not avoid accountability. It makes accountability constructive. The question is not, “Who failed?” The better questions are: Was the expectation clear? Was the workflow realistic? Was the team trained and supported? Did leadership follow through? What needs to change so the right action becomes easier next time? Blame shuts down learning. Accountability strengthens learning. Healthcare teams need standards, coaching, and systems that make consistent care possible. That is how accountability becomes a culture builder instead of a fear trigger.","Friday Leadership Reflection: Do your managers have time to coach the culture you want? Many organizations ask managers to improve patient experience, support staff, monitor metrics, resolve issues, and keep operations moving. The leadership question is not only whether managers know what to coach. It is whether the operating model gives them space to coach consistently. A culture of care needs leadership capacity, not just leadership intention.","Friday Field Note: Strategy succeeds or fails in the daily schedule. A patient experience strategy may be clear at the executive level, but the daily schedule determines whether teams can live it. Are there moments for communication? Is there time to recover after a service issue? Can staff complete follow-up reliably? Do managers have room to coach? Are expectations realistic during peak flow? Culture does not live in the strategy document. It lives in the workday. When the schedule leaves no room for care behaviors, the organization should not be surprised when those behaviors become inconsistent. Design the day to support the experience.","The Friday Fix: Take a 15-minute workflow walk. Choose one process and follow it in real time. Do not start with a meeting. Start with observation. Watch where staff pause, search, clarify, repeat, wait, or create a workaround. Then ask: What is making this harder than it needs to be? What does the patient experience because of it? What would make the right action easier? A short workflow walk can reveal more than a long report. Patient experience improvement often begins by seeing the work clearly.","What good looks like: patient flow that protects staff capacity. A well-designed flow does more than move patients faster. It reduces unnecessary confusion, rework, interruptions, and preventable escalation. Staff can focus. Patients receive clearer communication. Leaders see problems earlier. Teams have a shared understanding of what should happen next. Flow is not only a throughput issue. It is a care issue. When flow breaks down, staff absorb the friction and patients feel the impact. A culture of care designs operations so teams are not constantly recovering from avoidable breakdowns.","Friday Leadership Reflection: Is burnout being treated as an individual issue or a design signal? Resilience matters. Support matters. But if the same frustrations show up across teams, the organization should examine the work itself. What rework is constant? What processes create unnecessary emotional labor? Where do staff feel unsupported? Where does the patient experience depend on staff absorbing system friction? A culture of care must care for the caregivers by improving the conditions in which care is delivered. Burnout conversations should lead to operational questions, not only wellness reminders.","Field Lesson: Staff adoption improves when the workflow helps them too. What support will make the new behavior sustainable? A culture of care cannot be bolted onto the work. {"issues":[{"id":"8n71rill3ab","title":"Advancing With Intention: Career Direction, Brand, and Visibility","date":"2026-10-06","subject":"","preheader":"Career strategy, personal brand, LinkedIn, thought leadership, and sustaining development.","opening":"","sections":[{"id":"bbahs5ql3ab","heading":"","body":"","imageUrl":"","imageAlt":""}],"cta":"calendly","ctaHeading":"","ctaButton":"","closing":"","pillars":[],"values":[],"blogUrl":"","status":"draft","log":[]},{"id":"herz7i585ec","title":"From Touchpoints to Action: How to Build a Patient Experience Improvement Plan","date":"2026-10-13","subject":"","preheader":"","opening":"","sections":[{"id":"nszmvx185ec","heading":"","body":"You can finish a patient experience review with a page full of good ideas and still be unsure what to change on Monday morning. The phone system needs attention, patients are confused about parking, checkout instructions aren’t consistent, and the billing team keeps answering the same questions. Everything seems important, but the practice still has a full schedule to manage.

That’s where improvement can stall. Recognizing the problems is useful, but it doesn’t automatically give your team a manageable way to address them.

Throughout the *Nine Pillars of Patient Experience How-To series*, we’ve explored how to improve the eight patient touchpoints and nurture the long-term relationship those experiences can create. The next step is to turn that understanding into a plan.
You don’t need to launch eight projects at once. Choose a meaningful problem, understand where it begins, assign an owner, and see whether the changes make a difference for patients.

**Start with what patients are experiencing, not what you assume needs fixing**

Before deciding that your team needs another training session or your practice needs another technology platform, look closely at the problem you’re trying to solve.
Gather patient feedback, recurring complaints, operational information, and what staff hear every day. Ask your scheduling team what patients repeatedly need explained. Ask checkout staff which instructions they struggle to clarify. Ask the clinical team what questions come back after appointments.

The PX360 Assessment can provide a starting point for reviewing the journey, but use it alongside these other perspectives. Your team’s assessment of the experience shouldn’t replace the patient’s account.

Look for patterns without assuming that one review represents everyone. A complaint about an unanswered message deserves attention, but you’ll understand it better by checking how messages are assigned, how long they remain open, and what happens when the responsible person is absent.

The goal is to move from “Patients say our communication is poor” to a clearer understanding of what isn’t working.

**Choose one problem that’s specific enough to improve**

“Improve patient experience” is an intention, not an improvement plan. Even “Improve post-visit communication” leaves too much open to interpretation.

A more useful starting point is: “Patients are calling after their appointments because they don’t know when they’ll receive their results or who will contact them.”

Now the team has something concrete to investigate. You can review what patients were told, examine the follow-up process, and identify where expectations are missing or inconsistent.

When choosing your first priority, consider how much difficulty the problem creates for patients, how frequently it occurs, and what your team can realistically change. Don’t choose something simply because it’s easy to count or because one department is particularly vocal about it.

Urgent safety concerns need prompt attention through the appropriate clinical and safety processes; they shouldn’t wait their turn on a routine improvement list. For the remaining opportunities, choosing one manageable priority is more useful than announcing a broad initiative that no one has time to carry out.

You’re narrowing the work so you can address it properly, not declaring that the other problems don’t matter.

**Follow the problem across touchpoints**

The place where a problem becomes visible isn’t necessarily where it starts.
Consider an illustrative example: patients repeatedly call the front desk asking about results. The immediate response might be to tell the phone team to answer faster or create a new script. But the uncertainty could have begun during the clinical encounter, when the expected follow-up wasn’t explained. It could have continued through checkout, where no one confirmed how the patient would hear from the practice.
By the time the patient calls, the phone team is handling a problem created earlier in the journey.

Bring the people involved together and trace what actually happens. What does the clinician explain? What information reaches checkout? Who tracks the pending result? Who communicates the interpretation and next steps? What happens when the patient doesn’t use the portal?

Don’t ask staff to describe only what the policy says should happen. Ask them to walk through a recent example, including the workarounds they needed.

This is where collaboration becomes practical. Instead of asking one department to absorb the problem, the team can identify what needs to change across the handoffs.

**Put the goal, ownership, and review date in writing**

Once you understand the problem, write down what a better experience would look like.
For the results example, the goal might be that patients leave knowing how they’ll receive their results, the timeframe their care team has given them, and whom to contact with questions. That describes the patient’s experience rather than an internal task like “Update the after-visit summary.”

Then establish a baseline so you have something to compare against. Review a small sample of recent visits, examine related calls, and ask patients what they understood about follow-up. Use what you learn to set a realistic improvement target and a review date.

Assign one person to coordinate the work. That doesn’t mean one person does everything. The clinical lead should determine the appropriate clinical communication and escalation requirements, while administrative staff supports the scheduling, contact information, and handoff processes within their roles.

The coordinator’s responsibility is to keep work moving, surface obstacles, and ensure agreed-upon actions don’t disappear between meetings.

A useful plan can fit on one page. It should explain the problem, the experience you want to create, the change you’ll test, who’s responsible, how you’ll assess progress, and when you’ll review it. Accountability becomes much clearer when people can see those commitments in one place.

**Test a change before rolling it out everywhere**

You don’t need to redesign every appointment type or every location immediately. Start with a limited test that gives the team a chance to learn.

In the results example, one provider and their support team could test a consistent visit-close process. The clinician explains the follow-up plan, the patient receives that information in an accessible format, and the relevant details carry through to checkout. The practice also confirms who will track the outstanding work.

Giving patients a contact number helps, but it shouldn’t make them responsible for noticing when the practice hasn’t followed through.

During the test, pay attention to what makes the process difficult. Perhaps the instructions are buried in a lengthy summary. Perhaps the checkout team can’t see the information until after the patient has left. Perhaps a portal-only approach doesn’t work for some patients.

Those findings are reasons to adjust the process, not to blame the people trying to use it. Empathy means considering what the experience requires of the patient. Compassion means responding when the process creates a burden they can’t reasonably manage.
Staff needs the same consideration. A change that depends on someone completing another task without time, access, or backup needs more work before it becomes a standard.

**Check whether patients feel the difference**

A completed template doesn’t tell you whether a patient understands the plan. It tells you that a template was completed.

Look at the change from several angles. Did the agreed process happen? Did patients receive clearer guidance? Did the change create additional delays or an unmanageable workload elsewhere?

For the results example, review whether you communicated follow-up expectations and ask a sample of patients, “What were you told about how and when you’ll hear about your results?” That gives you more information than a yes-or-no question about whether everything was clear.

You can also track calls asking about results or next steps, using comparable periods and accounting for visit volume. But don’t assume fewer calls automatically mean better communication. Patients might understand more, or they might be having trouble reaching you. Interpret the numbers alongside what patients and staff tell you.
A small test gives you information to work with. It doesn’t prove that the process will work equally well for every patient, provider, or location. Use the findings to refine the change before expanding it.

**Make the improvement part of everyday work**

When a change appears useful, decide what will keep it working after the initial attention fades.

Update the workflow, include it in onboarding, clarify backup coverage, and set a regular review point. Make sure new staff can understand the process without relying on someone who happens to remember how the project started.

Also tell the team what you learned. Explain what patients found clearer, what still needs attention, and which staff suggestions improved the process. That makes the work more meaningful than announcing a new requirement.

As the first improvement becomes reliable, select the next priority. Over time, those changes can strengthen the connections between touchpoints without overwhelming the practice with competing initiatives.

The ninth pillar, *the long-term relationship*, remains the cumulative outcome you’re working toward. A short project can’t establish that you’ve earned someone’s loyalty. It can reduce confusion, demonstrate follow-through, and give patients another reason to trust the practice.

**Bring one clear priority to your next team meeting**

You don’t need a perfect dashboard or a practice-wide retreat to begin. Bring one recurring patient problem, ask the people involved to explain how it happens, and agree on a small change worth testing.

That work makes a Culture of Care tangible. Accountability means commitments are kept. Collaboration means people solve problems across departments. Compassion and empathy mean the patient’s circumstances remain part of the decision.
The Nine Pillars framework helps you see where the experience takes shape. An improvement plan turns that perspective into something your team can act on, and something patients can feel.

**Take the PX360 Assessment**

Where should your practice begin?
Take the PX360 Assessment as a starting point for reviewing the experience across all eight patient touchpoints. Pair your findings with patient feedback and staff insight, then bring one clearly defined improvement priority to your next team meeting.
You don’t have to fix the entire journey at once. Start with one Moment that Matters, make the experience more reliable, and build from there.
